concepts.title: Numbers worth memorizing
concepts.body: 1 day = ~86,400 s (round to 100k). 1M req/day ~ 12 QPS; 100M/day ~ 1.2k QPS. Peak is typically 2–5x average. Memory read ~100 ns, SSD random read ~100 µs, same-datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-region ~50–150 ms. A single modern Postgres node handles roughly 5–20k simple QPS; Redis ~100k ops/s; Kafka partitions ~10–50 MB/s each. 1 KB x 1B = 1 TB. Powers: 2^10 ~ 1e3, 2^20 ~ 1e6, 2^30 ~ 1e9.

concepts.title: The 45-minute shape
concepts.body: 0–5 min: requirements and scale. 5–10: API and data model. 10–20: high-level design with the core read and write paths. 20–38: deep dives (data layer, scaling hot spots, failure handling, the AI-specific parts). 38–45: bottlenecks, monitoring, trade-offs recap, what you would build next. Say 'I'm going to assume X, tell me if wrong' rather than asking open-ended questions every time.

concepts.title: Cache strategies and their failure modes
concepts.body: Cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss reads DB and fills cache. Simple, but stale reads and stampedes. Write-through: write cache and DB together; consistent but slower writes. Write-back: write cache, flush async; fast but risks data loss. Stampede fixes: request coalescing (single-flight), probabilistic early refresh, jittered TTLs, serve-stale-while-revalidate. Hot keys: replicate key across shards, local in-process cache with tiny TTL. Always say what happens when the cache is cold or down: the DB must survive it, or you need load shedding.

concepts.title: Consistent hashing
concepts.body: Map nodes and keys onto a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys instead of nearly all with modulo hashing. Virtual nodes (each physical node owns many ring positions) smooth load and let heterogeneous machines take proportional shares. Used in Dynamo, Cassandra, memcached clients, CDNs, and sticky routing of LLM requests to GPU pods that hold a warm prefix cache.

concepts.title: CAP, stated correctly
concepts.body: When a network partition happens, a system must choose between consistency (linearizability: refuse some requests) and availability (every non-failed node answers, possibly stale). Without a partition you can have both; PACELC adds that even then you trade latency against consistency. CAP is about behavior during partitions, not a permanent label on a database, and 'consistency' means linearizability, not ACID's C.

concepts.title: Quorums
concepts.body: With N replicas, writing to W and reading from R guarantees read-your-latest-write overlap when R + W > N. N=3, W=2, R=2 tolerates one node failure for both reads and writes. Quorums alone do not give linearizability: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums and hinted handoff, and clock-based LWW can still produce stale or lost data. Strong guarantees need consensus (Raft/Paxos) or careful read repair plus versioning.

concepts.title: Sagas instead of distributed transactions
concepts.body: A saga splits a business transaction into local transactions, each with a compensating action. Orchestration (a central coordinator) is easier to reason about; choreography (events) is more decoupled but harder to follow. Requirements: every step and compensation must be idempotent and retryable, and you must accept intermediate visible states. This is the exact pattern for multi-step agent workflows that touch external systems: book flight, book hotel, and if the hotel fails, cancel the flight.

concepts.title: Fencing tokens
concepts.body: A client holding a lease can pause (GC, network) past expiry while another client acquires the lock. Without protection both write. A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number issued with each lock grant; the storage layer rejects writes carrying a lower token than the highest it has seen. This makes the lock safe regardless of timing.

concepts.title: Distributed rate limiter design
concepts.body: Algorithm: token bucket per key (refill rate + burst). Implementation: Redis with an atomic Lua script (GET tokens/timestamp, refill, decrement) keyed by user/API key; sharded by key hash. Trade-offs: central Redis is accurate but adds ~1 ms and a dependency; local limiters with periodic sync are fast but allow overshoot; sticky routing keeps counts local. On Redis failure choose fail-open (availability) or fail-closed (protect backend) by endpoint risk. For LLM products, limit on tokens and concurrent requests, not just request count, and enforce cost budgets per tenant.

concepts.title: Retry amplification
concepts.body: If each of 3 layers retries 3 times, one user request becomes 27 attempts on the bottom service exactly when it is struggling. Mitigation: retry only at one layer, use retry budgets (e.g. retries <= 10% of requests), exponential backoff with full jitter, propagate deadlines, and make servers shed load fast with 429/503 + Retry-After. This applies directly to LLM providers during rate-limit storms.

concepts.title: News feed: fan-out trade-off
concepts.body: Fan-out on write pushes each new post into followers' precomputed feeds (fast reads, expensive writes, wasteful for inactive users). Fan-out on read assembles at request time (cheap writes, slow reads). Hybrid is standard: push for normal users, pull for celebrities (millions of followers) and merge at read time. Feeds live in Redis lists/sorted sets capped to N items; posts stored separately and hydrated by ID; ranking is a separate service.

concepts.title: Payments: never double charge
concepts.body: Client sends an idempotency key; server stores key → result atomically with the charge attempt. Use a double-entry ledger (immutable append-only entries that sum to zero) rather than mutating balances. State machine per payment (created → authorized → captured → settled / failed / refunded). Call external processors with their idempotency keys, handle unknown outcomes by querying status before retrying, and reconcile daily against processor reports. Outbox pattern publishes events reliably.

concepts.title: Design a ChatGPT-like service (outline)
concepts.body: Requirements: streaming chat, history, multiple models, 10M DAU, p95 TTFT < 2 s. API: POST /conversations/{id}/messages with SSE response; GET history. Edge: CDN/WAF, auth, per-user rate limit on requests, tokens and concurrency. Chat service (stateless) builds the prompt from stored history + system prompt + retrieved memory, truncating or summarizing to the window, then calls an inference router. Router picks model/pool by tier, load and prefix-cache affinity (consistent hash on conversation ID) and does admission control with queues and priority for paid users. GPU pools run vLLM-like engines with continuous batching, autoscaled on queue depth and KV-cache pressure. Tokens stream back through SSE; a stream-persistence step writes the final message to the DB (partitioned by user, e.g. Postgres/Cassandra/Dynamo) asynchronously, with a recovery path if the client disconnects (generation continues, client resumes by message ID). Safety: input/output moderation in parallel with generation, with the ability to cut the stream. Observability: TTFT, tokens/s, queue time, error rate, cost per conversation. Failure modes: GPU pool saturation (shed free-tier traffic, degrade to smaller model), provider/model outage (fallback), hot conversations, abuse (denial-of-wallet).

concepts.title: Design an LLM gateway
concepts.body: Responsibilities: unified API across providers, authentication and per-key/team budgets, rate limiting by tokens and concurrency, routing and fallback on errors/latency, caching (exact and semantic with strict scoping), request/response logging with PII redaction, cost attribution, guardrail hooks, retries with jitter and circuit breakers per upstream, and streaming passthrough. Data plane must be stateless and horizontally scalable with a small hot-path footprint (budgets in Redis with async reconciliation to a durable ledger). Control plane (config, keys, policies) stored in Postgres and pushed to data-plane nodes. Key trade-off: strict budget enforcement (central counter, more latency) vs approximate enforcement (local counters, overshoot).

concepts.title: Enterprise RAG platform: the hard parts
concepts.body: 1) Connectors and incremental sync (webhooks/cursors) with deletes propagated. 2) Permissions: store source ACLs as metadata and filter at query time (pre-filter in the vector DB, or over-fetch then post-filter with a permissions service); handle ACL changes without full re-index. 3) Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vectors, RRF) then cross-encoder rerank on top ~50. 4) Tenant isolation: per-tenant collections/namespaces or row-level filters, encryption keys per tenant. 5) Evaluation: golden queries per tenant, retrieval recall@k, faithfulness judged continuously. 6) Freshness vs cost: tiered indexing, embedding batch jobs, blue-green index swaps when the embedding model changes. 7) Citations and refusal behavior.

concepts.title: Voice agent latency budget
concepts.body: Target ~800 ms mouth-to-ear. Endpointing/VAD ~200 ms, streaming ASR final ~100–200 ms, LLM time-to-first-token ~250–400 ms (small/fast model, cached prefix, co-located), TTS first audio chunk ~100–200 ms, network ~50–100 ms. Techniques: stream every stage, start TTS on the first sentence/clause, speculative generation while the user is still finishing, keep models and media server in one region, WebRTC transport, barge-in handling that cancels the LLM and TTS pipeline instantly.

concepts.title: Agent runtime with durable execution
concepts.body: Model each agent run as a workflow: the orchestrator is deterministic code; each LLM call and tool call is an activity whose result is recorded in an event history. On crash, replay history to rebuild state and continue from the last completed step. Side-effecting tools get idempotency keys derived from (run_id, step_id) so a retried step cannot double-execute. Human approval becomes a signal the workflow waits on for hours or days at zero compute. Cost: history size grows, so compact long trajectories and store large payloads in blob storage by reference.

concepts.title: Sandbox platform for code-running agents
concepts.body: Isolation: microVMs (Firecracker) or gVisor, not plain containers, because the code is untrusted. Lifecycle: warm pool of pre-booted VMs for sub-second start, snapshot/restore to resume a session's filesystem and memory, hard TTLs and resource quotas (CPU, RAM, disk, wall time, process count). Network: default-deny egress, allow-list through a proxy that injects credentials (the sandbox never sees secrets), log all requests. Files: mount repo read-write on an overlay, persist artifacts to object storage. Scaling: bin-pack on bare-metal hosts, autoscale pool on demand, evict idle sessions. Security review checklist: escape surface, side channels between tenants, metadata endpoint blocking, noisy neighbor limits.

concepts.title: Deep research agent architecture
concepts.body: Lead agent plans and decomposes the question, spawns N sub-agents in parallel, each with its own context window and search/fetch tools; sub-agents return compressed findings with sources. A synthesis step writes the report; a citation/verification agent checks claims against sources. Infrastructure: task queue with concurrency limits, per-run token and time budgets, shared scratch store (memory) so the lead can persist its plan when its context fills, result caching of fetched pages, rate limiting per domain, and trajectory logging for eval. Trade-offs: multi-agent uses several times more tokens than single-agent chat, so reserve it for high-value, parallelizable questions.
